Mutiny Without a Captain: What I Found When I Sat Down With Every Department

Millions in revenue were leaking. Every department had a convincing explanation for why it wasn't theirs. Here is the 60-day journey from that room to a plan — and why the fix starts in the C-suite, not in the technology.

LW
Lisa Warren
Founder & CEO, Neural Horizons AI · October 21, 2026 · 7 min read

Day 1 · The diagnosis

The blame circle: every arrow points next door

Six teams. Six convincing stories. Millions leaking, and not one arrow points at the centre.

I walked into a large regional enterprise. A strong brand. National reach. Capable people. Eleven departments, and one question for each of them:

What is holding this business back?

Within an hour I had my answer. I didn’t get it from a report or a dashboard. I got it from how each team talked about the others.

Key Takeaways

  • Blame is data. When a team spends twenty minutes explaining why a problem belongs to someone else, it is showing you exactly where ownership is missing.
  • The facts always agree. We tested every story against the company’s own transaction records. The data confirmed the people, and it was blunter than they were.
  • The technology was not the constraint. Of eight agentic AI use cases tested, none was blocked by the technology. Leadership was the bottleneck.
  • The first fix costs a signature, not capital. One definition for every shared term and one named owner for every number.

Day 1The room

Sales blamed supply chain. Supply chain blamed planning. Planning blamed finance. Finance blamed IT. IT blamed the business.

Every team had a story. Every story pointed next door. Nobody pointed at themselves.

Day 15Blame is data

People assume resistance is noise. I treat it as a map. The blame points to the weak link every time, and a deeper dive only proves it.

“Leaders need to lead and stop hiding. The facts always come out. I can sit with each department, hear how they talk about the others, and see the weak links straight away. It isn’t rocket science, and a deeper dive only proves it.”

— Lisa Warren, Founder & CEO, Neural Horizons AI

I have seen this pattern across the Gulf, and I would bet you have seen it in your own building. It is not a regional quirk. It is what happens when no one is steering.

Day 30The data agrees

Opinions are cheap, so we tested every story against the company’s own records: hundreds of thousands of transaction lines covering real orders, real stock and real cancellations. The data did not just agree with the people. It was blunter.

  • Three departments used the same term. None of them meant the same thing.
  • Three versions of the forecast were circulating. Each one protected a different team.
  • Orders were being raised against stock that wasn’t there.
  • Nobody could name which product earned the company the most.
  • A major system migration was planned on top of processes nobody had ever mapped.
  • Of every risk we identified, almost none had ever been costed.

Millions in revenue were leaking between the departments. Every one of them could tell you, convincingly, why it wasn’t theirs.

Day 45A mutiny with no captain

Everyone knows the story of the Bounty: a crew turns on its captain. This was stranger. This was a crew with no captain to mutiny against, on a ship taking on water. They weren’t fighting the hole. They were documenting, in great detail, why the hole wasn’t theirs.

That is what a blame culture is. Every individual response is rational. The ship still sinks.

Leaders build it without meaning to. Every time a leader accepts “that’s not our department” as an answer, the culture grows another layer of cover.

Day 60Where AI comes in, and where it doesn’t

Most companies reach for the technology first. We did the opposite. We tested eight agentic AI use cases against four conditions that must be true before any agent is trusted with live operations:

  1. The data exists and is reachable.
  2. The terms it acts on are defined.
  3. A named business owner signs the boundary it operates within.
  4. It does not depend on the system migration.

The finding surprised the room. None of the eight was blocked by the technology. Two could start immediately. Five were waiting on a definition or a decision. One was waiting on data nobody had released. The agents were not the constraint. Leadership was. (We use the same four-gate method on every engagement; see We Evaluated 8 AI Agents for a Client. Only 2 Passed.)

What we would build on solid ground

Once ownership and definitions are in place, this is where AI earns its keep:

  • A knowledge agent grounded in the company’s own documents (RAG). It retrieves from internal records, emails and process files, and cites its source for every answer. Institutional knowledge stops living in people’s heads and messaging groups, so it stays when they leave. Nothing is invented.
  • A network and cost-to-serve agent. It reads route, depot and customer data to show where delivery is costing more than it earns.
  • A validation agent. It applies one agreed definition to every cancelled order and flags the reasons behind it.
  • A contribution agent. It shows profit by product and channel, so volume grows only where it pays.

Every agent runs under human oversight, inside a boundary a named owner has signed. Supervised autonomy, not a black box.

Built on solid ground

The plan: 100 days, in the right order

  1. Governance. One definition for every shared term. One owner for every number.
  2. Value. Know what earns before adding volume.
  3. Visibility. The data already exists. Read it.
  4. Real-time response. Adjust while the day is still running.

Three of the four steps need capital. One needs a signature. Start there.

Why this can’t wait

The data is becoming readable by everyone. AI makes it easy to see what used to stay buried. A leader who relied on opacity will lose it.

Agentic AI exposes weak ownership fast. An agent needs defined terms, a named owner and a clear boundary. Put one on a blame culture and it will not fix the culture. It will run the confusion at machine speed. (I wrote about who owns the decision when an agent acts in AI Agents Can Be Responsible. They Can Never Be Accountable.)

The facts come out. The only choice a leader has is whether to surface them first.

Related reading Breaking Down Silos with Agentic AI →

For CEOs, CFOs and boards: the 5-minute test

Put these five questions to your leadership team and time the answers.

  1. Which product or channel earns us the most margin?
  2. Who owns the definition of our most-used operational term?
  3. Which forecast is the plan of record?
  4. Can we see stock at the moment an order is taken?
  5. When something goes wrong, does the first conversation start with why, or with whose fault?

If three or more go unanswered, you don’t have a technology problem. You have an ownership problem, and it is costing you more than you think.
